devto.title: AI didn't make me a worse coder. It made me a worse reviewer.
devto.description: I built a lot of apps with AI last year and approved most of the code without really reading it. The research says the skill that decays isn't typing — it's the cognitive work underneath. Here's why every fix I've read (including my own first idea) is built to fail, and the one shape that isn't.

trends: Today's tech landscape highlights significant advancements and evolving challenges in AI, particularly regarding its integration into developer workflows and its societal impact. We see a strong push for AI in complex software engineering tasks, such as large-scale refactoring, alongside continued research into stable training of LLM critics and interactive world models with long-horizon memory. Concurrently, concerns about content authenticity and digital provenance are escalating, evidenced by invisible watermarking, raising questions about trust and privacy in AI-generated content. For developers, AI is shifting roles from pure coding to higher-level problem-solving and critical review, bringing to light a 'reviewer bottleneck' and a potential decay in human oversight skills. This shift fuels interest in advanced developer tooling, personal productivity optimization, and innovative ways to visualize and track individual performance and habits.

ideas.title: AI-Enhanced Code Provenance & Review Assistant
ideas.description: Develop a tool, either as a VS Code extension or a Git hook, that helps developers review code, especially changes suggested or generated by AI agents. This assistant would analyze diffs, flag sections that exhibit patterns common to AI generation, suggest specific areas for human scrutiny (e.g., complex logic, edge cases, security implications), and maintain a 'provenance log' for code blocks, indicating whether they were human-written, AI-generated, or AI-assisted. The goal is to combat the 'reviewer's cognitive decay' by providing targeted insights rather than just approving code blindly, ensuring robust review processes for AI-driven development.
tech_stack: Local LLM (e.g., via Ollama) or OpenAI API
ideas.source_inspiration: AI didn't make me a worse coder. It made me a worse reviewer.
steps: Set up a basic VS Code extension scaffold or Git pre-commit/pre-push hook.
Implement code parsing to analyze diffs and identify modified/added lines.
Integrate a heuristic or a local small language model to identify characteristics of AI-generated code.
Develop logic to suggest specific review points based on code complexity, identified patterns, or potential security vulnerabilities.
Design and implement a UI within the IDE (or a terminal output for Git hook) to display review suggestions and the provenance log.
Add functionality to store and retrieve provenance information for code sections (e.g., 'authored by GPT-4 at YYYY-MM-DD').

ideas.title: DevMind: Predictive Local Development Environment World Model
ideas.description: Inspired by 'ReWorld', this project aims to create a local 'world model' of a specific codebase and development environment. It would run as a background service or IDE plugin, observing developer actions (file edits, terminal commands, test runs, debugging sessions) within a project. Over time, it learns the project's structure, dependencies, and the developer's typical workflow. The 'DevMind' could then predict likely next actions, suggest relevant files or documentation, highlight potential side-effects of changes (especially during refactoring), and track progress across long-horizon tasks like a 'whole-repository stack migration' by understanding the project's evolving state and interdependencies.
tech_stack: IDE Extension API (e.g., VS Code Language Server Protocol)
Graph Database (e.g., Neo4j embedded, or custom in-memory graph)
Basic ML for sequence prediction or anomaly detection
ideas.source_inspiration: ReWorld: An Interactive World Model with Long-Horizon Memory
steps: Choose a target IDE and develop the skeleton for an extension or a standalone background service.
Implement listeners to capture relevant developer actions: file modifications, terminal commands executed within the project, and opened files.
Design a data model to represent the project's entities (files, functions, modules) and their relationships, along with a timeline of developer interactions.
Develop a 'project state' engine that updates the model in real-time based on observed actions and code changes (e.g., AST parsing for dependency updates).
Implement basic predictive heuristics: suggest files related to the current open file, or commands based on recent history and project context.
Create a simple UI within the IDE to display 'DevMind's insights, suggestions, or potential impact warnings.

ideas.title: Pro CLI: AI-Powered Terminal Productivity Dashboard
ideas.description: Build an advanced command-line interface tool that acts as a personal productivity dashboard. It passively tracks developer activity (e.g., time spent in specific project directories, commit frequencies, distinct commands used, active sprint tickets). Leveraging simple local AI models or rule-based systems, it provides personalized productivity insights, suggests 'wrong-sounding-but-effective' tips tailored to the user's observed patterns, and visualizes trends directly in the terminal using ASCII charts and color gradients. This tool would help developers understand their work habits, identify bottlenecks, and make data-driven improvements to their workflow.
tech_stack: Rich (for rich terminal output and charts)
ideas.source_inspiration: I Added Terminal Charts to My Dev.to CLI. Here's What My Data Looks Like.
steps: Choose a language (e.g., Python) and set up a basic CLI application structure.
Implement shell hooks (e.g., in `.bashrc` or `.zshrc`) to log terminal commands, current working directory, and timestamps to a local SQLite database.
Develop commands to query and visualize this data directly in the terminal using `Rich` for bar charts, sparklines, and trend indicators.
Implement a 'insights' module that uses simple rules or basic data analysis (e.g., clustering common commands, identifying peak activity times) to offer personalized productivity tips.
Add a feature to manually input and track daily/weekly goals and show progress against them.
Expand the data collection to include more sophisticated metrics, like commit message analysis for sentiment or task context.

quick_actions: For your next code review involving AI-generated content or a significant refactor, dedicate an explicit 20% more time than usual to scrutinize the underlying logic, edge cases, and architectural implications, focusing on *why* the code works rather than just *what* it does.

Identify one 'wrong-sounding' productivity tip (e.g., 'procrastinate strategically' or 'take more unscheduled breaks') and consciously apply it to a task this week, observing its impact on your focus and output without judgment.

Before writing any new code today, spend 10-15 minutes sketching out the high-level system design or the problem's core logic. Aim to reduce the total lines of code needed by focusing on modularity, leveraging existing solutions, and clearly defining the desired outcome.

Set up a simple local script or shell alias to log your most frequently used terminal commands and active project directories for a day. Review the output at the end of the day to identify patterns in your workflow and potential areas for automation.
